title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
What happened?


We added nonlinear transformations of the input (\(x^2\), \(x^3\), \(\sin(5x)\))

But the model is still a linear model

Why? Because it is linear in the parameters (\(\beta\))

The formula is still: \(y = X \beta\)


This is just feature engineering

We create new features from \(x\)

The model fits a linear combination of these new features

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
What happened?

All these transformations ONLY create new \(X\) such that this new \(X\) is linear with respect to the parameters \(\beta\), not the original input \(x\).

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
If We Had Magical Knowledge…


We could create the perfect set of features from \(input\)
And model ANY relationship between input and output no matter how complex it is!!

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
But we don’t


Sadly we don’t know the true function behind the data

So we have to guess the right transformations

Or create algorithms that can learn the right features/transformations for us

Isn’t that just: \[
\hat{y} = w w_1 x_1 + w b + b'
\]
So we’re back to a linear model!

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
section: How to fit our model (simple case)
text:
How to fit our model (simple case)



Any machine learning algorithm has a loss function.

It tells us how wrong our prediction is.
Let’s say for linear regression we have

\[
  \hat{y}_i = b + w_1 x_i
\]

For linear regression, we usually use:
\[
\text{Loss} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
This is called the mean squared error (MSE).

Our goal: minimize this loss by changing parameters in this case \(b\) + \(w_1\).







%%| mermaid-format: png

graph LR
  %% Input node
  X1(["$$x_1$$"])

  %% Output node
  Y(["$$\hat{y} = w_1 x_1 + b$$"])
  L(["$$\text{Loss} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$$"])
  

  %% Connection with weight label
  X1 -- "$$w_1$$" --> Y
  Y -- "$$\hat{y}$$" --> L

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
How to optimize \(w_1\)


let’s start with a random value for \(w_1\) and calculate the loss \[
  \text{Loss} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
\[
\text{slope} \approx \frac{\text{Loss}(w_1 + \varepsilon) - \text{Loss}(w_1)}{\varepsilon}
\]
Then:

If the slope is positive, that means the loss is going up ⇒ decrease \(w\) left
If the slope is negative, that means the loss is going down ⇒ increase \(w\) right

\[
\text{If} \quad \frac{\text{Loss}(1.01) - \text{Loss}(1)}{0.01} = 5 \quad \Rightarrow \text{decrease w}
\]
\[
\text{If} \quad \frac{\text{Loss}(1.01) - \text{Loss}(1)}{0.01} = -5 \quad \Rightarrow \text{increase w}
\]

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
Gradient Descent


We want to minimize the loss function:
\[
\text{Loss} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
For linear regression:
\[
\hat{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i
\]
The gradient of the loss with respect to parameters is:
\[
\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \beta_0} = \frac{-2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)
\]
\[
\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \beta_1} = \frac{-2}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)x_i
\]
We update parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient: \[
\beta_j \leftarrow \beta_j - \eta \cdot \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \beta_j}
\] where \(\eta\) is the learning rate.
Keep doing that until you cannot do better!!

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
section: Blame the hell out of parameters!
text:
Blame the hell out of parameters!

Gradient descent is a game of parameter blame.
Imagine we want to optimize \(w\)
Let’s start with our loss:
\[
\text{Loss} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
We ask two simple questions:
What’s wrong?
Who is to blame for it?
What’s wrong?

\(\text{Loss}\) is wrong.


Who is to blame for it?


\(\hat{y_i}\), our prediction is to blame
so we write \[
\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \hat{y}_i}
\]

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
section: Blame the hell out of parameters!
text:
Blame the hell out of parameters!

Let’s start with our latest blame!
\[
\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \hat{y}_i}
\] \(\hat{y}_i\) was not alone doing bad!
What’s wrong?

\(\hat{y}_i\) is wrong.


Who is to blame for it?


\(w\) was wrong because we calculate \(\hat{y}=wx+b\)
so we write \[
      \frac{\partial \hat{y}_i}{\partial w}
     \]

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
Putting it all together

This is how we calculate the gradient for \(w\) \[
      \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w}=\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \hat{y}_i} .\frac{\partial \hat{y}_i}{\partial w}
\] and we can do the same for \(b\)
\[
\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial b}
= \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \hat{y}_i}
\cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}_i}{\partial b}
\]

  Y(["$$\hat{y} = w_2 a + b_2$$"])

  X1 -- "$$w1$$" --> A1

  X2 -- " was affected by " --> X3

  






This is called the chain rule!

text:
Summing up so far



We define a machine learning model that helps us engineer features so we can do linear models to get a good fit

  %% Edges from inputs to hidden unit

  %% Edge from hidden unit to output
  A1 -- "w2" --> Y
  









We can use gradients to see the effect of all the parameters such as \(w\) and \(b\) on our accuracy \[
\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_1} = \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial a} \cdot \frac{\partial a}{\partial z_1} \cdot \frac{\partial z_1}{\partial w_1}
\]




We now know a mean to update the weights using gradient decend

\[
  w_j \leftarrow w_j - \eta \cdot \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_j}
\]

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
How to fit this model







%%{init: {"theme": "default", "themeVariables": { "fontSize": "24px" }}}%%
graph LR
  %% Input nodes
  X1(["$$x_1$$"])

  %% Hidden unit with color (middle unit)
  A1(["$$a=max(0,z_1=w_1 x1 + b_1)$$"])
  style A1 fill:#d2e3f5,stroke:#2b6cb0,stroke-width:2px,text-align:right

  %% Output node
  Y(["$$\hat{y} = w_2 a + b_2$$"])

  %% Edges from inputs to hidden unit
  X1 -- "$$w1$$" --> A1

  %% Edge from hidden unit to output
  A1 -- "w2" --> Y
  









Initialize the parameters to something random and pick a learning rate




Run the model (do all the calculations) to get \(Loss\). This is called forward pass




Calculate gradient for all the parameters \[
\frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_1} = \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial a} \cdot \frac{\partial a}{\partial z_1} \cdot \frac{\partial z_1}{\partial w_1}
\]



Update all the parameters using
\[
  w_j \leftarrow w_j - \eta \cdot \frac{\partial \text{Loss}}{\partial w_j}
\] This is called backward pass


Keep going until you cannot make the \(Loss\) smaller! This is your simple neural network!

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
What is a Neural Network?



A neural network is just a fancy function approximator or feature engineering machine.

It’s made by stacking layers of tiny models.

Each unit does the same thing:

Take a weighted sum

Add a bias

Apply a non-linear function (like ReLU)


Together, they can model very complex curves.

Formally, a simple one-hidden-layer neural network looks like:
\[
\hat{y} = w_2 \cdot \text{ReLU}(w_1 x_1 + b_1) + b_2
\]
It’s still made of linear parts! We just hide them inside activations!

  Y(["$$\hat{y} = w_2 a + b_2$$"])

  X1 -- "$$w1$$" --> A1

  %% Edge from hidden unit to output
  A1 -- "w2" --> Y

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
In Practice: Many Choices


Neural networks come with many choices:
Activation functions:

ReLU: \(\max(0, x)\)
Sigmoid: \(\frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}\)
Tanh: \(\tanh(x)\)
GELU, Leaky ReLU, Swish…

Loss functions:

MSE (regression)
Cross-entropy (classification)
Contrastive

Architectures:

Fully connected (MLP)
CNN (images)
RNN, LSTM, GRU (sequences)
Transformers (language & more)

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
section: Example: Neural Network for Regression in R
text:
Example: Neural Network for Regression in R


We’ll use the keras package to fit a small neural network.
Task: Predict \(y = x^2\) from noisy observations.
Model: - 1 hidden layer with ReLU - MSE loss - Optimizer: SGD
library(keras)
set.seed(123)
# Prepare data for keras
x_train <- matrix(x, ncol = 1)
y_train <- matrix(y, ncol = 1)

# Build model
model <- keras_model_sequential() %>%
  layer_dense(units = 10, activation = "relu", input_shape = 1) %>%
  layer_dense(units = 1)

# Compile and fit
model %>% compile(
  loss = "mse",
  optimizer = optimizer_sgd(learning_rate = 0.05)
)

model %>% fit(x_train, y_train, epochs = 100, verbose = 0)

# Predict and plot
y_pred <- model %>% predict(x_train)

Example: Neural Network for Regression in R


We’ll use the keras package to fit a small neural network.
Task: Predict \(y =  sin(2 * pi * x) + 0.5 * sin(4 * pi * x)\) from noisy observations.
library(keras)
set.seed(123)
# Prepare data for keras
x_train <- matrix(x, ncol = 1)
y_train <- matrix(y, ncol = 1)

# Build model
model <- keras_model_sequential() %>%
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu", input_shape = 1) |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dense(units = 1)

# Compile and fit
model %>% compile(optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 1e-3), loss = "mse")

model %>% fit(x_train, y_train, epochs = 500, verbose = 0)

# Predict and plot
y_pred <- model %>% predict(x_train)

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
Example: PCA using neural networks


We’ll use the keras package to do a PCA
library(keras)
library(mixOmics)
data("nutrimouse")
set.seed(42)
X <- nutrimouse$gene

# Normalize the data
X_scaled <- scale(X)

n_input <- ncol(X_scaled)
n_pcs <- 2  # Number of components (like nPcs)

# Build encoder
encoder <- keras_model_sequential()  %>%
  layer_dense(units = n_pcs, activation = "linear", input_shape = n_input)

# Build decoder
decoder <- keras_model_sequential() %>%
  layer_dense(units = n_input, activation = "linear", input_shape = n_pcs)

# Connect into autoencoder
input <- layer_input(shape = n_input)
encoded <- encoder(input)
decoded <- decoder(encoded)

autoencoder <- keras_model(input, decoded)

# Compile
autoencoder %>% compile(
  optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.05),
  loss = "mse"
)

# Train
autoencoder %>% fit(
  X_scaled, X_scaled,
  epochs = 200,
  batch_size = 32,
  verbose = 0
)

# Extract the "scores" (PCs)
scores <- predict(encoder, X_scaled)

title: Introduction to Neural Networks
text:
Final Tips: Architecture & Training Choices


How many layers?

Start small: 1–3 hidden layers is often enough
More layers = more abstraction, but also more training trouble

How many neurons per layer?

Try 16–128 per layer
Too few = underfitting

Too many = overfitting / slow

Which activation?

ReLU = default for deep nets

Tanh = smooth regression

Softmax = classification

Never use activation after last layer if you’re predicting a number (regression)


Which optimizer?

adam: works well 90% of the time

sgd: good for theory, but slow

rmsprop: good for RNNs

What not to do:

Don’t add activation = "relu" in the output layer of a regression
Don’t use too many layers without regularization
Don’t forget to normalize your input!

What helps:

Normalize or standardize input

Use dropout or early stopping for regularization

Plot training + validation loss to detect overfitting
